title: Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology
answer: Detection and triage, synthetic imaging, 3D anatomical models, ultrasound enhancement and radiomics.

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage covers AI systems that examine medical images to flag suspected abnormalities and reorder radiology worklists by urgency.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the creation of new medical images that resemble real patient scans but are generated by computational models rather than acquired from a patient.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in diagnostic imaging and radiology involve converting patient-specific imaging data, typically CT or MRI, into physical replicas of organs, bones, vessels, or pathology.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers AI systems that assist clinicians at the bedside with acquiring, interpreting, and acting on ultrasound images.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images, turning regions of interest into structured data for analysis.

sections.body: This field applies artificial intelligence to medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasound. The work includes detecting abnormalities, sorting scans by urgency, generating new images from existing ones, building three dimensional models for surgery or printing, improving bedside ultrasound, and extracting quantitative features from images. In practice, AI systems now flag possible fractures, lung nodules, brain bleeds, and breast lesions in real radiology workflows. Some tools also create synthetic contrast images or reduce scan time by reconstructing missing data. The focus is on assisting radiologists and other clinicians, not replacing them.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has moved beyond research into limited clinical use, but it is not solved. Many detection models perform well on narrow tasks with clean data, yet they can fail on rare conditions, different scanners, or patient populations not seen in training. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models overall, though only some are for diagnostic imaging, and it also tracks 801 scientific models, which shows a large research base but not equal clinical maturity. Synthetic imaging and radiomics remain mostly experimental, with questions about reproducibility and whether the extracted features add reliable value. The site also records 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, a sign that real failures carry serious consequences. Honest limits include the need for human review, the risk of overdiagnosis, and the lack of long term outcome data.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section break the field into five practical areas. Pathology Detection and Scan Triage covers the most mature use, where AI flags likely disease and orders worklists by urgency. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans explains how models create new views or reduce radiation dose, while Anatomical Models and 3D Printing turns scan data into physical or digital structures for planning. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement focuses on making handheld ultrasound easier for non specialists, and Radiomics describes the extraction of many quantitative features from images for research. A reader would start with Pathology Detection and Scan Triage for current clinical reality, then move to Synthetic Imaging and Anatomical Models for emerging applications, and finish with Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement and Radiomics for more specialized or experimental work.
